newsitem.title: UK: HORSE RACING-BOOKIES STILL COUNTING COST OF DETTORI SEVEN-TIMER.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-BOOKIES STILL COUNTING COST OF DETTORI SEVEN-TIMER.

text.p: British bookmakers were still counting the cost on Sunday of Frankie Dettori's historic Ascot seven-timer but three half-millionaires have already emerged.
Some estimates suggest that as much as 18 million pounds ($28 million) will have been taken off the bookmakers by backers supporting the champion jockey in doubles, trebles and accumulators.

Rob Hartnett, a spokesman for Coral bookmakers, said on Sunday: "We are still trying to sort through the bets. The problem we face today is that many shops were pretty much cleared out last night and the banks don't re-open until tomorrow.
"We have one client who won 259,000 pounds ($404,000) and that is our biggest single loss so far.
"The atmosphere in the shops for the last race was incredible with most clients cheering Frankie home. Indeed, anyone shouting for Pat Eddery's mount which finished second were being booed."
Despite the losses, Ladbrokes spokesman Mike Dillon described the day as a "great" one for racing and the betting industry.
"As far as I know we have two clients who have won 500,000 pounds ($780,000), one in central London and one in Ireland," said Dillon.
"But it was a great day which should lead to the best Sunday raceday ever from a betting viewpoint.
"I would expect punters to be queueing to get into the shops today." Racing was taking place at Ascot again on Sunday with Dettori back in the saddle once more.
A William Hill client in Morecambe, northern England, was also celebrating a 500,000 pounds success thanks to Dettori's magnificent seven, which came to cumulative odds of over 25,000-1.
Hill spokesman David Hood has described Saturday as "the worst day in bookmaking history."
The winner from Morecambe, Darren Yates, 30, a joiner, picked up his winnings on Sunday and then said: "It's just marvellous. I'm going to put exactly the same bet on again."
Yates laid out 62 pounds ($96) on Saturday on a bet known as a Super Heinz -- a mixture of combination bets linking seven horses -- and collected 550,820 pounds ($859,900).
His wife, Annaly, said: "I don't mind him betting, but I wasn't so keen on him putting on the bet yesterday morning because 60 pounds is a lot of money for us."
